t: IDEA BOX ANSWERED - K BASELINES AND PITCHER TYPES, BOTH TESTED
x: Two sharp K-model questions from the idea box, both taken seriously. One: 'are strikeout averages derived off all pitchers or just starters?' Good catch - the league baseline the model shrinks toward does come from batters' totals against ALL pitching, relievers included, and relievers strike out more hitters than starters do. So we rebuilt the model with a starters-only baseline and re-scored three weeks of held-out starts: the result was identical to three decimals, with essentially zero bias either way. The reason it doesn't matter: the model combines pitcher, lineup, and league in a ratio, and the same baseline appears on both sides - it cancels. Fair question, clean answer, nothing to fix. Two: 'factor in the TYPE of pitcher - a groundball guy versus a strikeout guy - not just his K rate.' We added each starter's contact-allowed profile (hits per batter, season to date) as a second identity factor at several strengths: at best it tied the plain model, at worst it hurt. The pitcher's strikeout rate, anchored across two seasons, already carries who he is; a second fingerprint added nothing the first didn't. Both ideas are logged in the permanent inbox with their verdicts. Keep them coming - a question that makes us re-check a baseline is worth as much as one that ships.

t: K WATCH: CLOSING-LINE VALUE TRACKING ON, TWO MORE FORM IDEAS TESTED
x: Three follow-ups from tonight's autopsy discussion. One: the K list now captures each game's closing strikeout prices about an hour before first pitch and grades every model lean against the close - closing-line value, the metric professionals trust most, because beating the close shows real information long before win-loss records mean anything. It appears in the K footer as the sample builds. Two: current form was retested properly - a pitcher's last five starts blended into his season rate at every weight, and the opposing team's strikeout rate over the last two and three weeks in place of season numbers. Heavier recent form was clearly worse (the fourth time recency has failed a test in this project), team form was worse at every window, and a light 25% seasoning of last-five form was an exact tie on accuracy with a small gain on side-picking - not a win, so nothing ships; the weekly retrain will keep re-checking it. Three: the honest answer to 'what would the model have hit all season?' - against REAL lines we only have three days (50%, that is the whole problem); against a proxy line built from each pitcher's season average, the model called the right side 60.2% of held-out starts. That number flatters: a proxy line has no vig and none of the books' lineup and pitch-count information. The gap between 60% against arithmetic and 50% against the market IS the market's skill.

t: K LOSS AUTOPSY - THE ANSWER WAS IN THE DATA, AND THE ANSWER IS VARIANCE
x: After pulling the K texts we did what we did for the main model's cold streak: put every loss under the microscope, this time down to the individual pitch. Every graded start was split into two error sources - how many batters the pitcher faced (workload) and how often he struck them out (rate) - and 49 starts were joined to the actual pitch-by-pitch record: every whiff, called strike, foul, and the night's velocity against the season's. Findings: the workload model is genuinely good (off by 0.6 K); nearly the whole miss lives in the night's strikeout rate (1.7 K); and that 1.7 sits exactly at the mathematical noise floor of a single start - a pitcher facing 22 batters at a 20% K rate produces +-1.8 K of pure randomness no model can remove. The books sit at the same floor. Wins and losses carried identical edges and mirror-image rate errors, and the losses left no pre-game fingerprint: velocity, zone rate, called strikes all identical between winning and losing nights. What decides these bets is the night's swing-and-miss, which nothing measurable beforehand predicts. One weak corner logged honestly: the model's OVER leans went 8-16 while unders went 24-20, consistent with its slight high bias that the weekly retrain is already correcting. Verdict: not missing data - variance on a no-edge tie. The way to ever beat this market is price, not prediction, and the display-only ruling stands.

t: TWO IDEA BOX REQUESTS SHIPPED SAME DAY
x: Both of yesterday's idea-box submissions are live. One: the K WATCH footer now reports the average miss ON THE BOOK'S LINE, not just on the outcome - and it is a perfect illustration of why the K texts came off: actual strikeout totals land 1.76 K from the line on average, but only +0.01 K toward the model's side. The model reads the totals almost exactly as well as the books do; neither side owns the coin flip, and the vig eats the tie. Two: BULLPEN RANKINGS - all 30 pens ranked by recent quality (7-day ERA and WHIP, save conversion) plus tonight's fatigue from the pitch-by-pitch usage archive: pitches thrown the last two days, arms likely unavailable, and how many of each team's six most-used relievers are rested. Reader context only, with the warning printed right on it: the model uses none of this - bullpen inputs were tested four separate times and failed out of sample every time. Keep the ideas coming; they are archived permanently now and every one gets an answer here.

t: K PLAY TEXTS PULLED - THE LEDGER SAID NO
x: Three days ago strikeout leans started going out as texts, with a public tripwire: they live or die by the Props Ledger. The ledger has spoken - 82 graded starts, 26-28, minus $544 at flat stakes, negative in every edge bucket including the largest edges, which is the signature of a model whose disagreements with the book are the book's information, not ours. The model's strikeout PREDICTIONS are fine (off by about 1.6 per start); its edges against the prices are not real. So K WATCH returns to display-only: the list stays up, grades itself nightly, and retrains weekly. The texts come back only if the card earns it. Also fixed today: idea-box submissions were passing through a message service that only keeps things for 12 hours - they are now archived permanently the moment they arrive, and two ideas already in the queue (average miss vs the line, bullpen rankings) are logged.

t: WEEKLY RETRAINS FOR THE PROP MODELS - THE WATCH LISTS NOW LEARN
x: The main model has retrained every week since launch; the K, Hit and Long Ball models had not - their settings were fit once in the spring and frozen, so a model drifting (say, projecting strikeout totals a shade too high, which the K list did in its first two days: 4.3 projected vs 4.0 actual per start) had no way to correct itself. Fixed at the root: every Thursday morning each prop model refreshes its full-season data, refits its settings on a rolling window (everything through three weeks ago, tested on the most recent three weeks), and the live lists read the refit the next morning. Same discipline as the main engine: the retrain has to prove itself out of sample every week, and every parameter change is logged. First refit ran tonight.

t: NEW ON THE BOARD - SOCCER (PREMIER LEAGUE), REFERENCE NUMBERS ONLY
x: A soccer tab, up in time for the Premier League opener on Friday. It is a goals model: every club carries an attack and a defence rating fitted on every result since 2015 with recent form weighted more, built on expected goals (shot quality) blended with actual goals. Those two ratings give an expected scoreline, and everything on the card - win / draw / win, double chance, over-under, both teams to score, the three most likely scores - is read off that one score grid, laid beside Pinnacle with the vig removed and the best price from DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM and Caesars. The rules are the same as MMA: it was tested walk-forward, refit before every match date across six seasons and 2,280 matches, and it did not beat the closing line - log-loss 0.979 against the market's 0.963. We also tried starting from the market's own Friday price and letting the model nudge it; that did not beat the Friday price either. Calibration is honest (it says draw 23%, draws happen 24%), but calibration is not an edge, and we say so on the page. So: reference numbers, no plays, no stakes, nothing texted. Newly promoted clubs carry a prior until they have played and are flagged on the card. Matchweek 1, all ten fixtures, is up.

t: THE PROPS LEDGER - THE WATCH LISTS NOW HAVE A REPORT CARD
x: The Long Ball, Hit, and K watch lists have always graded themselves every night; now the grades are public, built exactly like the full-game LEDGER. For each list: calibration by probability bucket (when the model said 15%, did it happen 15% of the time?), the published top-15 versus what the model expected, home/away splits, who is beating or trailing their model number the most, active streaks, and a flat-$100 paper line against the best book price. First card, Long Ball Watch after five graded days: calibration is tight through the 5-20% range where nearly all listed hitters live; the published list has produced 11 homers against 15.8 expected - a slow start, tracked honestly; and the paper-vs-market line is negative, as it should be for a model built from the same public numbers the books use. The other two cards fill in as their archives grow. Display-only remains the rule; a report card is how a watch list would ever earn more than that.

t: NEW ON THE BOARD - K WATCH
x: A third daily list, this one for the pitchers: every probable starter's strikeout total tonight as a full distribution - the chance of clearing every half-line from 2.5 up - laid beside the real strikeout lines and prices from DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM and Caesars. Same rules as the other two watches: it was tested walk-forward on 2,575 starts from this season (May and June to fit it, July onward held out) before it went up, and only what survived is in the number - the pitcher's strikeouts per batter (this season, anchored to last year so a short 2026 sample can't run away), the strikeout tendency of the nine hitters he faces (his opponent's most recent lineup in the morning, the confirmed lineup once it posts), and how many batters he is likely to face, mostly from his last five starts. On the held-out months it missed the strikeout total by 1.8 per start against 1.9 for simply using his season average and 2.1 for the league average, and its probability at the book's line landed within about three points of reality across the buckets. Things that were tried and did NOT beat the plain version out of sample, so are not in the number: recent form, hitters' splits against lefties and righties, the opposing lineup's on-base rate, and a career-long anchor instead of last year. Each row shows the model's expected strikeouts, the books' line with the model's fair price for the over and under, each book's prices, and MODEL LEANS - the single over or under, book and line where the model's chance most exceeds what the price implies. Tap a row for the pitcher's season line, the model's inputs, and the ladder of every half-line with the best book price on each side. Every starter is graded overnight against the boxscore and the footer keeps the honest running paper record of the model's lean at the logged price - morning prices and lineup-lock prices separately - published good or bad. Expect the model to lean under more often than over: strikeout props are priced toward the over because that is what the public bets. Display only, no bet flags, nothing texted, and it stays that way unless the paper record earns otherwise.

t: NEW ON THE BOARD - HIT WATCH
x: A second daily list joins Long Ball Watch: each hitter's chance of recording at least one hit today, with his two-hit chance alongside. Same discipline as the home-run list - it was tested walk-forward on 22,000 starter-games from this season before it went up, and only what survived that test is in the number: the hitter's season hit rate (shrunk toward league average so a hot fortnight can't fake its way up), the opposing starter's hits-allowed tendency, the ballpark, and how many trips to the plate he really gets. That last part is the lesson from the test: hitters get pulled, pinch-hit for, or run out of at-bats more often than a schedule suggests, so the list is built on the trips they actually average, tightened to the batting slot once lineups post. Recent form and the pitcher's strikeout rate were tried and failed the test, so they stayed out. Book prices sit next to the model's fair price where posted; expect the books to be shorter - hit props are heavily juiced toward the favorite - and read gaps as entertainment. Display only, no bet flags, graded nightly like everything else.

t: STARS PULLED CLOSER TO THE PACK - HR MODEL SHRINKAGE TIGHTENED
x: Follow-through on this morning's autopsy. The one real miss was the elite tier: the very best power hitters were rated about five points too high. The dial that controls that is how hard the model pulls every hitter's season rate toward league average before trusting it - it was set so a hitter needed roughly 200 plate appearances to be believed halfway; it is now 300. Tested walk-forward, the tighter setting halved the elite over-rating and scored better on the most recent two months, but slightly worse on the two before that - a split decision the rules would normally leave alone. The owner made the call to move it, on the grounds that every independent check so far (night one, the season backtest, the 882-homer autopsy) has pointed the same direction. Effect on the board: the top of the list comes down about a point - Schwarber 22.9% instead of 24.2% - and the model's fair prices sit a touch closer to the sportsbooks. The nightly grading is the jury; if the earlier months turn out to be the truth, this moves back.

t: HOME RUN AUTOPSY - 882 HOMERS, PITCH BY PITCH, AGAINST THE MODEL
x: We pulled every home run of the last month - 882 of them - with the pitch that was hit, its speed, where it crossed the plate, who threw it, and what the model gave that hitter that morning. What we learned. WHERE THEY COME FROM: homers are democratic - a third of them came from hitters the model rated 8-12%, and one in ten came from hitters under 8%. Only 7% came from the 20%+ tier the top of the board is made of. So even a perfect list of the fifteen best is watching a small slice of the night's homers; that is the nature of the event, not a flaw. THE PITCH: 35% four-seam fastballs, then sliders, sinkers, changeups - and the model was NO more surprised by any pitch type than another (mean rating within a point across all of them). Same for velocity, count, inning, and zone: 92% of homers came from inside the strike zone, a quarter from dead center, and the model's confidence was flat across all of it. Translation: there is no hidden pitch-level pattern the model is blind to. THE REAL MISS: the elite tier. Hitters the model rated 1.7x the league homered 18% of the time against a predicted 23% - about five points hot, the same tail overshoot the backtest flagged. We tested the obvious fixes walk-forward: pulling stars harder toward league average helped the recent months but hurt the earlier ones - a split decision, so no change; and weighting hot recent form (the Tatis and Merrill months) added nothing at any strength - the third time recency has failed a trial here. Verdict: model unchanged, but the elite over-rating now has a specific candidate fix waiting on more evidence, and the nightly grading is the jury.

t: ARSENAL AND WEATHER BACKTESTED - BOTH BENCHED. THE LIST GETS SIMPLER AND HONESTER
x: Round two of the walk-forward backtest put yesterday's shiny new features on trial: the pitch-arsenal matchup and the wind/temperature adjustments. We rebuilt point-in-time arsenal profiles for every hitter-day (what he had done against each pitch type BEFORE that morning, never after) and pulled the actual game-time weather for all 1,816 games. The verdict was unanimous and humbling: every one of them improved the months they were fitted on and got WORSE on the July-plus holdout - at full strength, half strength, and quarter strength. Wind and heat, the most physically obvious effects in baseball, most likely fail because the season's own scoring environment already absorbs them, and what's left after the ballpark factor is noise. So all of it comes out of the published number, same as the platoon factor before it. What remains is what survived: the hitter's own power, the opposing starter, the ballpark, and his batting slot. The wind and heat badges stay on the board as context - clearly separated from the math. And here's the payoff you can check yourself: with the failed factors stripped out, the model's FAIR prices now land within a few ticks of the sportsbooks on most hitters - two completely independent routes to nearly the same answer. Every factor is still logged nightly, so any of the benched ideas can earn its way back with a bigger sample. That's the whole system in one sentence: everything gets tested, and only what survives gets to touch the number.

t: LONG BALL WATCH BACKTESTED ON THE WHOLE SEASON - PLATOON FACTOR CUT
x: Rather than wait weeks for the nightly archive to fill up, we rebuilt the entire 2026 season point-in-time from pitch-level Statcast data and replayed the home-run formula walk-forward: 21,490 batter-games across 101 slates, every prediction using only what was knowable that morning. The verdicts. CALIBRATION: honest across the board - when the model said 12-16%, reality said 14%. A zero-homer top-fifteen night like Tuesday happens on 3-4% of slates even with a well-calibrated list; that one was mostly a bad beat. THE SURPRISE: the platoon factor - how a hitter fares against lefties vs righties, the most baseball-intuitive input on the card - made predictions WORSE in both the fit and holdout windows, and caused most of the top-of-list overconfidence. Home-run platoon splits are simply too noisy at season sample sizes, the same lesson recency weighting and bullpen stats taught us. So it is cut from the published number - though still logged nightly, so the future trained model can re-litigate it with more data. WHAT SURVIVED: the hitter's own power rate does most of the work; the opposing starter and the ballpark each add a real sliver. The remaining watch item: the very top of the list still runs about two points hot, and every night's grading keeps the receipts.

t: LONG BALL WATCH 2.0 - PITCH ARSENALS, LINEUPS, AND TEMPERATURE
x: Night one graded rough: the top fifteen went 0-for-15. The autopsy was honest and useful. Across the whole slate the model was nearly perfect - it expected 29 homers, 29 flew - but the top of the list was overconfident, and 14 strong predictions were on hitters who never even played. Three upgrades ship today. One: PITCH ARSENALS - using Statcast data, the model now knows which pitch types each hitter punishes and what mix the opposing starter actually throws; a slider-crusher facing a slider-heavy arm gets credit, a fastball hunter facing a changeup artist loses some. Two: LINEUP AWARENESS - the moment official lineups post, the list re-ranks itself: scratched or resting hitters drop off entirely, and confirmed hitters get their true batting-slot plate appearances (a leadoff man gets more chances than a nine-hitter). No more probabilities on players who are not playing. Three: TEMPERATURE - warm air carries the ball, so hot nights now boost the number and cold nights trim it, on top of the existing wind read. The overconfident-top-of-list finding stays under watch: every night's grading is banked, and if the top bucket keeps overshooting, the fix is already designed.

t: SHARPS LOST THEIR EDGE AT THE TRADE DEADLINE - VETO ON A 25-GAME TRIPWIRE
x: Follow-up to this morning's veto audit, and credit where due: a subscriber called the pattern before we measured it. Season-wide, the side professional money moved toward won 56.6% of games before the July 31 trade deadline - genuinely sharp. Since the deadline: 53.5%, a near coin flip that LOSES money at the prices. The veto's blocked bets flipped at the exact same line: before the deadline the veto saved $470; since, it has cost $329. The likely mechanism: half the league changed uniforms at the deadline, and the models behind sharp money need time to re-rate traded players - so August line moves carry less information than July ones did. Twelve post-deadline blocked bets is too small to act on, so the rule goes on a formal tripwire instead: if the post-deadline phantom ledger is still profitable at 25 blocked bets, the sharp-fade veto comes off and the change gets logged here.

t: SHARP VETO AUDITED - KEPT, BUT NOW ON THE RECORD
x: A subscriber asked the right question: is the sharp-fade veto actually helping? We graded every bet it ever blocked as if we had played it. Answer: the blocked bets went 10-12 for -141 dollars - so the veto has saved money overall, but far less convincingly than the brutal early evidence that created it (2-15 in paper trading). And the last week of blocked bets would have gone 5-2. Small samples both ways, so the veto stays - but it no longer gets to work in the dark. The phantom ledger of vetoed would-be bets now updates nightly and is published in THE SPLITS, and if it turns clearly positive over a real sample, the veto is gone. We also corrected the SHARP CONFIRMED explainer: season data says sharp agreement has not helped our plays, and the board now says so.

t: LONG BALL WATCH GOES LIVE - HOMERS LIGHT UP GREEN AS THEY HAPPEN
x: The home-run list now watches the games with you. Once first pitch goes, the board checks the live boxscores each minute - when a listed hitter goes deep, his row lights up green with a blinking marker (steady once his game is final; a second homer updates the count). Nothing about the predictions changes; this is the scoreboard half of a list that now keeps score. Watching which greens light up - and how often the top of the list cashes versus the bottom - is exactly the calibration story the training archive is quietly recording every night.

t: LONG BALL WATCH STARTS KEEPING SCORE - TRAINING DATA COLLECTION IS ON
x: The home-run list now grades itself. Every morning the system logs its full slate of predictions - all ~330 eligible hitters, every factor behind each number, and the sportsbook prices - not just the fifteen that make the board. Every night it checks the boxscores and records who actually went deep, who didn't, and who never played. That growing archive is the raw material for a REAL trained home-run model: today's version is honest arithmetic, but arithmetic can't learn which of its inputs matter most or how they interact - a trained model can, and it needs graded examples to learn from. This is the same playbook as the pitch-by-pitch bullpen archive: collect first, hypothesize later, and let every claim face graded results. The display doesn't change today. What changes is that from now on, every number the list publishes is on the record - and when there are enough graded days in the bank, the hand-built math has to beat what the data teaches, or it gets replaced by it.

t: BET WINDOW TIGHTENED TO 3-6% - THE DATA MOVED THE CAP
x: The play window was 3-8% since V2 launched, with the cap always described as humility, encoded. We regraded every tracked game by edge size at a finer grain, and the humility needed to move: 3-6% edges won 57.9% of 171 graded games and account for essentially all of the season's profit, while the 6-8% zone won just 47% of 100 and lost money - the 7-8% slice was the worst bucket on the whole curve at 42%. So the cap comes down from 8 to 6, effective today. What this means for you: slightly fewer plays, and the plays that survive come from exactly the zone that has been paying all season. The honest footnote: the 6-7% sliver graded mildly positive on its own, but 43 games is too thin to hang a rule on - if the curve says it earned its way back in a few hundred games from now, the window can move again. Same discipline as ever: the window is built on graded results, not on how confident the model feels.

t: LONG BALL WATCH - DAILY HOME RUN PROBABILITIES ON THE BOARD
x: New section on the board: the fifteen hitters most likely to go deep today, with the model's probability for each and real sportsbook prices next to it. The math is simple and fully inspectable: the hitter's season home-run rate (pulled toward league average so a hot week can't fake its way up the list), how he hits the opposing starter's throwing hand, that starter's own home-run tendency, the ballpark he's hitting in tonight, the wind when it's blowing out or in at an open-air park, and how many trips to the plate he usually gets. FAIR is the model's number expressed as American odds; DK/MGM/CZR are the books' actual 'to hit a home run' prices as they post them. Two honest caveats ship with it. One: even the best slugger alive only homers about one day in four - the numbers look low because home runs are genuinely rare, not because the model is shy. Two: this is a DISPLAY, not a betting product - no bet flags, no texts, no ledger, and gaps between FAIR and a book's price are entertainment until this list has a graded record. Same rule as everything else here: if it ever wants to become a play, it has to earn that on paper first.

t: BULLPEN AVAILABILITY TESTED - NOT ADOPTED. THE BULLPEN CHAPTER CLOSES
x: The last and best version of the bullpen idea: not how good the relievers are, but which arms are actually AVAILABLE tonight. Using our new pitch-by-pitch usage archive (every reliever's workload, every day, all season) we measured each team's bullpen burden over the previous two days, counted tired arms (20+ pitches yesterday or back-to-back outings), and counted rested top arms. Walk-forward across 556 games: nothing. Burden was an exact tie with the model alone; every other version was slightly worse. That completes the bullpen family - quality (tested), exposure (tested), availability (tested) - four trials, zero survivors. The market prices bullpens fine; our edge lives in the starter innings, which is exactly what the F5 paper experiment exists to isolate. The usage archive keeps growing nightly regardless: good data outlives the hypothesis that ordered it.

t: F5 SHADOW RULES TIGHTENED - LOCKS WITH LINEUPS, FINDS ITS OWN WINDOW
x: Three upgrades to the first-5 paper experiment. One: paper flags now lock at the exact moment the real play locks - the lineup-confirmed evaluation. A pre-lineup F5 flag that does not survive that evaluation drops off the site and never enters the ledger, same rule as real leans. Two: only lineup-confirmed paper bets count in the record. Three: instead of assuming the full-game 3-8% betting window transfers to a different market, the ledger now grades EVERY locked game by edge size - so the first-5 market can reveal its own best window from live data. When the sample is big enough, the window we use will be the one the data chose, not the one we inherited.

t: BULLPEN EXPOSURE TESTED - NOT ADOPTED
x: A subscriber-grade idea: do not just measure bullpen quality - measure how MUCH bullpen each team will need. We estimated every starter's expected innings from his last five starts (the hook), multiplied the leftover innings by recent bullpen ERA, and asked whether that burden gap predicts winners on top of the model. Walk-forward answer: it makes the model WORSE - 3 to 4 points of accuracy worse - and the hook estimate alone was worse still. That is now three bullpen-family ideas tested and three rejections, which matches everything else we know: our losses are decided in the starter innings, not the late ones. The deeper version (which specific reliever enters, how rested each arm is, platoon-driven hooks) stays on the candidate list but needs months of usage data we are now positioned to collect. Meanwhile the F5 shadow IS the answer to this insight from the other direction: instead of modeling the innings we cannot see, bet only the innings we can.

t: F5 SHADOW LAUNCHED - FIRST-5-INNINGS MODEL ON PAPER
x: The loss autopsy showed our losses die early: games decided in the starter innings, exactly where the model's features live. Follow-up test: scored against 683 live games, the model predicts the FIRST FIVE INNINGS winner at 57.7% vs 53.2% for full games. Starters own innings 1-5; every inning after that adds bullpen noise the model does not handicap. So we built a second head: same four features, retrained to predict the first-5 winner, and pointed it at real first-5 moneyline prices from four books. The catch that keeps this on paper: F5 markets are priced off the same starter stats we use and charge about a point more vig, so higher accuracy does not automatically mean profit. It now logs shadow bets every slate - no money, no texts - and the ledger is public in THE LEDGER below. Decision after 50+ paper flags. The de-vig experiment taught us why: its backtest said +8.6%, its live ledger said no. Everything earns its way in live or stays out.

t: LOSS AUTOPSY - NO HIDDEN FLAW FOUND
x: We put every graded loss under the microscope looking for what they share: price range, edge size, home/away, claimed confidence, starter quality, bullpen freshness, lineup strength, park, line movement. The honest headline: losses look almost exactly like wins. The model was NOT more confident on its losses (53.7% claimed vs 54.7% on wins), edges were the same size, and starter metrics were nearly identical - there is no cluster of games where the model was fooled in a diagnosable way. One suspect did emerge: losses skewed toward games where the OPPONENT'S bullpen had been fresher over the prior week. So we ran the full walk-forward trial - does 7-day bullpen ERA improve predictions on top of the model? Answer: no. Slightly worse, in fact. Week-old bullpen ERA is too noisy to carry signal; the cluster was small-sample coincidence. What survives: a smarter fatigue measure (actual pitches thrown, days of rest) is still on the candidate list, and home-side plays running cooler than road plays stays on the watch list. Every suspicion gets the same trial; this one came back clean.

t: RECENCY WEIGHTING TESTED - NOT ADOPTED
x: Second feature idea of the day: weight pitcher stats toward recent starts (last-5 or decaying average) instead of full season. Tested on 649 games with true point-in-time data - only starts BEFORE each game counted. Result: pure recent-form was 2-3 points WORSE than season-to-date; blends were ties. Five starts of ERA is mostly luck - weighting toward it weights toward noise. The idea survives in better form: recent VELOCITY and swing-and-miss stabilize in a single game and can flag a declining arm long before ERA does. That version is on the candidate list with data collection underway. Every idea gets the same trial; most lose; the record is why.

t: SIERA/xFIP TESTED - NOT ADOPTED
x: A sharp outside suggestion: ERA describes the past; skill estimators like FIP and K-BB predict the future better. We ran the full walk-forward gauntlet on 3,454 out-of-sample games. Result: replacing our pitching feature with FIP or K-BB made the model 1.3-1.6 points WORSE; adding them alongside added nothing. Why: our pitching input was never raw ERA - it is capped to a plausible talent range and blended toward career numbers by sample size, which already removes most of the luck that skill estimators exist to remove. Every feature idea gets this same trial: beat the baseline out-of-sample or stay out of the model.

t: TRADE-DEADLINE PROOFING
x: Player stats follow the PLAYER, not the team - a traded pitcher's ERA, sample size, and a traded hitter's platoon numbers all travel with him automatically. But the league's data feed reports traded players in per-team chunks, and the model could previously read only the newest chunk - meaning a deadline acquisition might have been judged on 3 innings with his new club instead of his full season. Fixed everywhere: the model now always uses full-season combined numbers regardless of how many uniforms a player has worn. Shipped before any post-deadline slate was played.

t: COLD STREAK AUDIT - PROCESS HEALTHY
x: After a 1-7 stretch (-$600 over four days) we audited every play in the slump against the TRUE closing line, pulled from pre-pitch snapshots. All 8 plays beat the close, averaging +5.1% - the market moved toward our number after every single bet. The model's own probabilities expected ~4.4 wins from those 8 plays; getting 1 is a ~2% unlucky tail that any bettor eats a few times a season. Composition showed no pattern: losses spread across dogs and favorites, no team, no price band. Verdict: variance, not decay - no changes made. The tripwire that WOULD trigger changes: a slump arriving with negative closing-line value. This was the opposite.
